\chapter{Mine, Somebody Else's, And Which Kind}
\label{ch:propio-y-ajeno}
\hlchaptermodality{350}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say propio, ajeno, igual, distinto and el tipo, and say why English proper meant owned long before it meant correct.}

Complete ES-C350-tipo: mark a thing as yours or another's, as the same or a different one, and ask what sort it is.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[propio]{propio — one's own, and the owning inside \emph{proper}}

\label{lesson:ES-C350-propio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the anniversary}, then \emph{the diary}. (\emph{El aniversario}; \emph{la agenda}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item María · España · profesor — the names this word labels.
  \item la casa — the sort of thing you say it about.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PRO-pio}, two beats with the weight on the first. \emph{-pio} is one glide, not two beats. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{propio} — \textquotedblleft{}one's own.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish already has \emph{mi}, \emph{tu}, \emph{su}. \textbf{Propio} is what you add when \emph{su} is not emphatic enough: \textbf{su propia casa}, \emph{her own house} — hers and nobody else's.

Latin \textbf{proprius} meant exactly that: belonging to the individual rather than held in common. The old guess at its make-up is \textbf{prō prīvō}, \emph{for the private one}.

English took it and let it drift a long way. \textbf{Proper} meant \emph{owned} first — a \textbf{proper noun} is a name that belongs to one thing only, which is the original sense sitting in plain sight. \textbf{Property} is what you own. A \textbf{proprietor} owns it. To \textbf{appropriate} something is to make it your own, and it is impolite for exactly that reason.

Only later did \emph{proper} slide into \emph{correct}, by way of \emph{fitting, belonging to this occasion}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to say a thing is yours and not somebody else's.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{propio}
  \item \emph{mi propia casa}
  \item \emph{su propio libro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did English \textbf{proper} mean before it meant correct? (Owned.) And what is a \textbf{proper noun}, on that older sense? (A name belonging to one thing only.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ajeno]{ajeno — somebody else's, the exact opposite of \emph{propio}}

\label{lesson:ES-C350-ajeno}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the diary}, then \emph{one's own}. (\emph{La agenda}; \emph{propio}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item otro — the other one this belongs to.
  \item alguien — the somebody in question.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-JE-no}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{j} is scraped at the back of the throat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ajeno} — \textquotedblleft{}somebody else's,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}not mine.\textquotedblright{}

English has no single word for this. It says \emph{someone else's}, three words where Spanish uses one: \textbf{una casa ajena}, a house belonging to another person.

Latin \textbf{aliēnus} is built on \textbf{alius}, \emph{other}. And Latin had two words for \emph{other}, used carefully: \textbf{alius}, another out of many, and \textbf{alter}, the other of exactly two.

Spanish inherited both. \emph{Otro} comes down from \textbf{alter} — the other one of a pair. \textbf{Ajeno} comes from \textbf{alius} — belonging to some other person out there, unnamed.

English took \emph{alius} whole and never softened it. An \textbf{alien} is from elsewhere. To \textbf{alienate} somebody is to make them another person's problem. An \textbf{alias} is your other name, and an \textbf{alibi} is the plea that you were \emph{elsewhere}.

Together with \emph{propio}, you can now sort the world into mine and not-mine.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two sides of ownership, in one word each.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ajeno}
  \item \emph{una casa ajena}
  \item \emph{propio o ajeno}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word for \emph{other} is inside \emph{ajeno}? (\emph{Alius}.) And what does an \textbf{alibi} claim? (That you were elsewhere.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[igual]{igual — the same, from a surface with no tilt}

\label{lesson:ES-C350-igual}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{one's own}, then \emph{somebody else's}. (\emph{Propio}; \emph{ajeno}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item todo — the whole this measures against.
  \item la manera — the thing two people can do equally.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{i-GUAL}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{gua} is one glide, and the \emph{g} is hard. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{igual} — \textquotedblleft{}the same,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}equal.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{aequus} did not mean \emph{identical}. It meant \textbf{level} — a plain with no slope, a scale with neither pan down, water lying flat.

\textbf{Aequālis} is what has that levelness, and Spanish wore it into \textbf{igual}.

Hold on to the flatness and the English family falls open. The \textbf{equator} is the line that levels the globe into halves. An \textbf{equinox} is the day whose night is level with it. To be \textbf{adequate} is to come up level with what is needed. \textbf{Equity} is fairness weighed on a level scale. \textbf{Equanimity} is a mind that does not tilt.

Two everyday Spanish uses to keep. \textbf{Es igual} means \emph{it's all the same}, a polite shrug. And \textbf{igual que} compares: \emph{igual que ayer}, the same as yesterday.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to say two things match.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{igual}
  \item \emph{es igual}
  \item \emph{igual que ayer}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{aequus} mean? (Level, with no tilt.) And what does the \textbf{equator} do to the globe? (Levels it into halves.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[distinto]{distinto — a different one, marked apart with a pin}

\label{lesson:ES-C350-distinto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{somebody else's}, then \emph{the same}. (\emph{Ajeno}; \emph{igual}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item otro — the plain way to say another one.
  \item el modo — one of the things that can differ.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dis-TIN-to}, three beats with the weight on the second. Both consonants of \emph{-st-} are sounded. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{distinto} — \textquotedblleft{}different,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}a different one.\textquotedblright{}

You have \textbf{otro} for \emph{another}. \emph{Distinto} is sharper: not merely a second one, but one that is unlike the first.

Latin \textbf{distinguere} is \textbf{dis-}, \emph{apart}, plus an old verb \textbf{stinguere}, \emph{to prick}. Marking things apart meant putting a pinprick beside them — a tally, a dot, a small wound in the wax.

So a \textbf{distinct} thing is one somebody has pricked apart from its neighbours, and to \textbf{distinguish} is to do the pricking.

The family is odd and worth having. To \textbf{extinguish} is to prick a flame out. An \textbf{instinct} is an urge that pricks you from inside. Something \textbf{distinguished} has been marked off from the crowd.

In use, remember that \emph{distinto} usually goes after its noun — \textbf{un libro distinto} — while \emph{otro} goes in front.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Same, and not the same, in one pair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{distinto}
  \item \emph{un libro distinto}
  \item \emph{igual o distinto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{stinguere} mean? (To prick.) And what does it mean to \textbf{extinguish} a flame, on that picture? (To prick it out.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el tipo]{el tipo — the kind, and the dent a hammer leaves}

\label{lesson:ES-C350-tipo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the same}, then \emph{a different one}. (\emph{Igual}; \emph{distinto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cosa — what has a kind.
  \item la manera — the near neighbour of this word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TI-po}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{t} is made with the tongue against the teeth, not the ridge behind them. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tipo} — \textquotedblleft{}the kind,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the sort.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{týptein} was \emph{to strike}, and a \textbf{týpos} was first the \textbf{blow}, then the \textbf{dent the blow left behind}.

Watch it move. Strike a coin with a die and the coin carries a \emph{typos}. Strike a thousand coins with the same die and every one carries the same mark — so the word slides again, from the single dent to \textbf{the pattern all the dents share}. That is a \emph{kind}.

English follows the whole path. Movable \textbf{type} is metal that strikes paper. \textbf{Typography} is writing by striking. Something \textbf{typical} matches the pattern. A \textbf{prototype} is the first strike, and a \textbf{stereotype} was a printing plate cast solid so it could never be re-set — which is why calling a thought a stereotype is an insult.

One warning. In everyday Latin American speech \emph{un tipo} also means \emph{a guy}. It is casual; it is not for strangers.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to pin down which one: yours, another's, the same, a different one, and what sort it is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el tipo}
  \item \emph{un tipo de libro}
  \item \emph{¿qué tipo?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{týpos} first? (A blow, and then the dent it left.) And what was a \textbf{stereotype} before it was an insult? (A printing plate cast solid.)
\end{tcolorbox}
